newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish Solidarity may picket over privatisations.
newsitem.headline: Polish Solidarity may picket over privatisations.

text.p: Solidarity chief Marian Krzaklewski said the trade union might deploy pickets outside some major firms to prevent their hasty privatisation by the ruling ex-communists before a general election due around September.
PAP news agency quoted Krzaklewski as telling union delegates in southeastern Poland on Saturday that the government planned faster privatisation of some large firms.

He said Solidarity leaders were considering the possibility of organising pickets in front of these enterprises to prevent what he termed a further plundering of the nation's wealth, the agency reported.

Krzaklewski is the dominant figure in the Solidarity Election Action (AWS) alliance of dozens of right-leaning parties that have grouped together to try to beat the ruling Democratic Left Alliance (SLD) at the parliamentary polls.

Solidarity chiefs say they favour privatisation but that in the form applied by the ex-communists it benefits only the current political elite rather than the mass of Poles, while revenues from such sales are used for vote-winning programmes.

The union wants a sweeping mass privatisation programme, while the ruling left has implemented one involving only about 500 small and medium-sized companies and has sold other firms or sectors off individually to investors.

AWS wants sales of major firms like banks, copper firm KGHM Polska Miedz and telecoms monopoly TPSA to combine offers to strategic investors with free shares for employees, the public and stakes set aside for pension funds.

"If, after the elections, the political set-up is favourable for us, the new government's first task will be to prevent the sale of major workplaces such as Polska Miedz or Telekomunikacja (TPSA)," PAP quoted Krzaklewski as telling the meeting in Rzeszow.

Krzaklewski appealed to his supporters to turn out in the nationwide referendum on May 25 and vote against a new draft Polish constitution which has been drawn up by the government and some opposition parties in parliament.
Solidarity has produced its own draft which emphasised Poland's patriotic and Catholic traditions rather than the more secular approach of the SLD-backed version.
